pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 9–11, Climate Zones — Earth has distinct zones (tropical, temperate, polar, arid/desert, mountain); which zone a place belongs to is set mainly by latitude and geography; each zone supports different ecosystems and ways of life.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS2 geography — describe and understand climate zones, biomes and vegetation belts; identify position of the tropics, Equator and polar circles.
• Standards — US (NGSS): 3-ESS2-2 '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-ESS2-2]' — the anchor; formalises the named-zone system built on Geography & Local Weather (7–9). State/regional tier DEFERRED.
• Operational details: teach zones as latitudinal BANDS (with altitude as the vertical exception) and connect each zone's climate to its characteristic ecosystem and human life; use a world map/globe so the banding is spatially anchored; stress that 'desert' means DRY not hot (cold deserts exist) and that mountains break the simple latitude rule.
• Checkpoint (Tier A|B|C): Tier A — name and describe four zones; Tier B — explain that latitude (plus altitude/geography) determines a zone and give an example of how a zone shapes its life; Tier C — explain exceptions (cold deserts, tropical mountains) and link zones to global patterns.
bestPractices: Present zones as latitudinal bands on a map/globe so the pattern (Equator → poles) is visible, with altitude as the vertical exception
Tie each zone to a vivid characteristic ecosystem and way of life (rainforest, savanna, tundra) so the climate→life link is concrete
Confront 'desert = hot' directly — desert means DRY; polar/high-altitude deserts are cold
Use the mountain zone to show latitude isn't the whole story (a tropical peak can be freezing)
Combine information from more than one source (map + climate data + biome images) to meet the 3-ESS2-2 'obtain and combine' practice
keyRepresentations: World map/globe banded into the climate zones by latitude
Zone cards pairing each zone's climate with its characteristic plants, animals and people
A latitude–altitude grid showing how both together place a zone
Drill-down biome scenes (rainforest, desert, tundra) revealing zone-shaped life
commonMisconceptions: All deserts are hot — 'desert' means dry; cold/polar deserts exist
Climate zones depend only on latitude — altitude and geography also set them (a tropical mountain can be cold)
Zone boundaries are sharp lines rather than gradual transitions
Temperate = boring/mild everywhere — temperate zones have strong seasons
A zone's plants/animals are there by chance rather than adapted to its climate

learn.summary: Learners aged 9–11 learn to name, locate and characterise Earth's climate zones (tropical, temperate, polar, arid/desert, mountain), explain that latitude plus altitude and geography set which zone a place belongs to, and link each zone's climate to its characteristic ecosystems and ways of life. Two targeted surprises — a cold desert and a freezing peak on the Equator — confront the 'desert = hot' and 'latitude is everything' misconceptions. A banded map/globe makes the Equator→poles pattern visible; drag-the-latitude sorting and matching tasks add active causal reasoning and assessment.

activities.title: Banded climate-zone atlas
feedback: If a learner says the Equator is hottest because it is 'closest to the Sun', point to the Equatorial mountaintop with snow: it is actually higher — nearer the Sun — yet freezing, which shows distance is not the cause. Its summit is cold because of its altitude; then explain the Equator→poles pattern by the angle at which sunlight strikes.
When a learner calls every hot place a desert, contrast the hot-and-wet rainforest band with the hot-and-dry desert — 'desert' means DRY, not hot (and cold deserts also exist).
If a learner treats a boundary as a sharp line, highlight that zones grade gradually into one another.
If a learner assumes temperate places are mild and uneventful, point out that temperate zones have distinct, changing seasons, and many temperate places have warm summers and cold winters.
Praise specifically when a learner connects a named zone to a concrete adaptation (e.g. tundra plants staying low against the cold) rather than just naming the zone.
activities.rationale: A classification/field-guide task where the latitudinal banding is literally the picture lets learners name, locate and characterise a fixed set of zones and link each to its life; combining map, data and images addresses the 'obtain and combine information' practice. The two counter-examples directly target the dominant misconceptions.
sourceClaims: DfE KS2 geography requires pupils to describe and understand climate zones, biomes and vegetation belts, and to identify the position of the tropics, Equator and polar circles.
Latitude is the primary control on climate zones, with altitude and geography as major modifiers; 'desert' denotes aridity, not heat (cold deserts exist).
learnerActions: Study a world map (or globe) split into coloured latitude bands — tropical hugging the Equator, temperate mid-latitudes, polar caps near the poles — and name each band.
Reveal each band's climate profile (e.g. hot-and-wet, moderate-with-seasons, freezing) and its characteristic plants, animals and ways of life.
Drill down from a band into a biome scene — steaming rainforest, baking desert, frozen tundra — and describe how the zone's climate shapes what lives there.
Sweep attention from the Equator to the pole and describe how the ecosystems transform in step with the climate.
Examine two deliberately placed surprises: a COLD desert (dry but not hot) and a freezing mountaintop sitting right on the Equator; explain why each breaks a simple rule.
Combine more than one source (banded map + climate data + biome images) to describe a chosen zone.
activities.intendedInsight: Climate zones are a readable global pattern, not a list to memorise: climate (set mainly by latitude, modified by altitude and geography) shapes the ecosystems and human life found in each zone.

activities.title: Drag the latitude and altitude — watch the zone change
feedback: If a learner expects a tropical latitude to always be hot, have them raise the altitude slider and watch the zone turn cold, then explain that the height, not the latitude, is doing this.
When a sorting placement is wrong, prompt: 'What is this creature's zone like — wet? dry? freezing? — and which band matches that?'
Confirm reasoning, not just the answer: ask the learner to state the determinant (latitude and/or altitude) behind each correct placement.
activities.rationale: Manipulating latitude and altitude and watching the zone (and its ecosystem) recompute makes the causal 'what determines a zone' explicit and tests the climate→life link actively, complementing the field-guide atlas.
sourceClaims: Latitude is the primary control on climate zones, with altitude and geography as major modifiers; 'desert' denotes aridity, not heat (cold deserts exist).
learnerActions: Move a marker to different latitudes and predict, then check, which climate zone results.
Add an altitude slider: raise the marker on a tropical latitude and observe the zone shift toward cold/alpine, discovering that height can override latitude.
Sort animals, plants and types of home into the zone where they belong, and justify each placement by the zone's climate.
Build a case that shows latitude alone is not enough (e.g. a tropical peak that is freezing because of its altitude).
activities.intendedInsight: Latitude is the main control on a place's climate zone, but altitude can move a place into a colder zone, and geography (such as distance from the sea or mountains blocking rain) can make a place drier or give it more extreme seasons — so two places at the same latitude need not share a zone.

activities.title: Why is the Equator hot? — the angle-of-sunlight investigation
feedback: If a learner holds the 'closest to the Sun' idea, run the torch demo: the beam's spread, not the tiny distance difference, explains the heat.
If a learner reports today's weather, clarify that a climate zone is the typical pattern over many years, not a single day.

When a learner explains the Equatorial snow by ALTITUDE — a high summit is cold even though the Equator's near-vertical rays make the lowlands hot — confirm this is the reasoning that marks real understanding; being near-vertical to the Sun does not keep a high peak warm.
activities.rationale: Addresses the row's key misconception that the Equator is hot because it is nearest the Sun, using the stated torch-on-globe demonstration to make ray-angle concentration tangible, while correctly attributing the Equatorial-mountain exception to altitude rather than ray angle.
sourceClaims: Latitude is the primary control on climate zones, with altitude and geography as major modifiers; 'desert' denotes aridity, not heat (cold deserts exist).
learnerActions: Discuss the prompt: 'The Equator is hot all year and the poles are freezing. Some say the Equator is hottest because it is the part of Earth closest to the Sun. Is that why?'

Shine a torch straight down onto a globe near the Equator, then shine the same torch at a slant near a pole while keeping it at the same distance from the surface, and compare how large an area the light spreads over.
Explain in your own words why slanted rays spread the same heat over a larger area and so warm it less.
Apply the ideas to the Equatorial snowy mountain: explain how a place on the Equator — where rays are near-vertical and the lowlands are hot — can still be freezing at its summit because of altitude.
Answer: why are the tropics hot ALL year while many temperate places have cold winters?
activities.intendedInsight: A place's climate zone is decided mainly by latitude through the ANGLE at which sunlight strikes — near the Equator rays hit almost straight down and concentrate heat on a small area, while near the poles they strike at a slant and spread over a larger area, so it is colder. The Equator is not meaningfully closer to the Sun. Altitude and distance from the sea are additional controls; altitude is why a peak on the Equator can be freezing even though its lowlands are hot.

activities.title: Zone-matching and latitude-sequence check
feedback: For the cold-place-near-the-Equator item, confirm that high altitude (or other geography) can make a low-latitude place cold, so latitude alone does not settle the zone.
If a sequence is mis-ordered, ask the learner to find the Equator first and work outward toward each pole.
On a wrong match, point back to the zone's defining climate (wet/dry, mild/extreme) rather than giving the answer outright.
activities.rationale: Matching, sequencing by latitude and targeted multiple-choice items map onto the evidence statements and probe the determinant and the exceptions, serving assessment. As a recognition/selection format it checks understanding but does not by itself elicit extended independent construction; pair it with the explanation and investigation tasks.
learnerActions: Match each zone to its description and to its characteristic plants, animals and ways of life.
Sequence a set of places by latitude from Equator to pole and predict each one's zone.
Answer multiple-choice items on 'what determines this zone?', including an item that describes a cold place near the Equator — decide what makes it cold.
Explain at least one example of how a climate zone affects the plants, animals or people living there.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can independently name and describe the zones, state what determines each, and reason about exceptions such as a cold place near the Equator.

activities.title: Voices from contrasting zones
feedback: If a learner attributes a lifestyle to chance, ask what the climate forces: 'What does this much rain / this much cold require of people and plants here?'
Encourage comparison across zones to surface the climate feature responsible for each difference.
activities.rationale: Hearing from people and wildlife in contrasting zones can humanise the climate→life link. It complements rather than replaces the map-based naming and locating that the atlas supports well.
learnerActions: Read or listen to short first-person accounts from people (or wildlife descriptions) living in contrasting zones — e.g. a rainforest, a cold tundra, a hot-dry desert.
Ask and answer questions about how the zone's climate changes daily life, food, shelter, or how plants and animals survive.
Compare two accounts and explain which climate features drive the differences.
activities.intendedInsight: A zone's plants, animals and people are shaped by (adapted to) its climate, not there by chance — the climate→life link made human and concrete.

constraints: Teach tropical, temperate and polar zones as broad latitudinal BANDS (Equator→poles), with altitude (mountain zone) and geography such as distance from the sea, rain shadows and dry subtropical belts (which help explain where deserts form) as exceptions to a purely latitude-based pattern, and keep them spatially anchored on a map or globe.
Stress that 'desert' means DRY, not hot: cold/polar and high-altitude deserts exist.
Use the mountain zone to show latitude is not the whole story — a tropical peak can be freezing because of its altitude, even though its lowlands are hot.
Distinguish a climate zone (typical pattern over many years) from today's weather.
Present zone boundaries as gradual transitions, not sharp lines.
A matching/multiple-choice check confirms recognition and reasoning but does not on its own elicit extended independent explanation; pair it with the explanation and investigation tasks.
A zoned globe is genuinely spatial and shows the banding wrapping the planet; it is an option for the classification task and offers a different spatial experience from a flat banded map.
Torch-and-globe demo is an approximation: the difference in distance to the Sun across Earth is negligible, so the demo should emphasise ray ANGLE and spread, not distance.
Attribute the Equatorial-mountain cold to ALTITUDE, not to ray angle; at the Equator the near-vertical rays warm the lowlands.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Of the three cited sources, only the NGSS 3-ESS2-2 claim is marked verified in the row; the DfE KS2 and Met Office/Köppen claims are marked unverified. Treat the latitude/altitude/desert-aridity principle as expert-stated but not independently verified here.

The original recommendation ranked a static banded image as 'ideal' and other formats by catalog fit; these rankings were removed. No format is asserted uniquely necessary — the alternatives (drag sliders, globe, conversation, matching quiz) are preserved as serving distinct purposes, each with untested efficacy.
The torch demo was tightened to stress spread/angle over distance so it does not reinforce a distance explanation.

The Equatorial-mountain exception is driven by altitude (temperature falls with height), not by ray angle; feedback in every activity (including the atlas rebuttal) was corrected so learners are not credited for attributing the summit's cold to ray angle.
Assessment-field internal references and two-tier labels were not carried into learner-facing actions; assessment content informs the diagnostic and matching tasks only.

probeDeeper: There's snow on a tall mountain right on the equator. If 'nearer the Sun' made places hot, how can that be?
Why is the tropics hot ALL year, but where you live has cold winters?
How does living in a polar zone change what plants, animals or people can do there?
assess.correctAnswer: No — the equator isn't meaningfully closer to the Sun. Climate zone is decided mainly by latitude: near the equator the Sun's rays hit almost straight down and concentrate heat on a small area, while near the poles the same rays strike at a slant and spread over a larger area, so it's colder. Altitude and distance from the sea also matter.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The equator is hot because it's the closest part of Earth to the Sun'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Shine a torch straight-on vs slanted onto a globe — slanted light spreads the same heat over more area.
errorPatterns.distractor: The equator is the part of Earth nearest the Sun.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: explains climate zones by distance to the Sun

errorPatterns.pattern: 'A climate zone is just what the weather is doing there today'
errorPatterns.nextMove: A zone is the typical climate over many years, not a single day.
errorPatterns.distractor: A place's climate zone is whatever the weather is like there today.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: reports today's weather instead of the long-run pattern

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Every hot place is a desert / all cold places are the same'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast a hot-and-wet tropical rainforest with a hot-and-dry desert.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: collapses distinct zones such as tropical-wet and arid

responseLevels.gap: Explains zones by nearness to the Sun; can't name or describe zones.
responseLevels.full: Names and describes zones, explains latitude (ray angle) plus geography as the determinant, and gives an example of how a zone shapes its ecosystems or ways of life — transferring to a case like equatorial mountain snow.
responseLevels.partial: Names four or more zones and links them loosely to 'near/far from the equator' but can't give the angle-of-sunlight reason, or confuses zone with today's weather.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: The area around the equator is hot all year, while the poles are freezing. Some children say 'the equator is hot because it's the part of Earth closest to the Sun.' Is that why? What really decides whether a place is in a hot, temperate, or polar climate zone?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks 'hot = nearer the Sun' cannot explain why the tropics stay hot year-round or why high mountains are cold; only the angle-of-sunlight/latitude account marks real understanding.
